planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring; in zone 9 plant March–May. Chestnut arose as a seedling of Suebelle and shares much of that cultivar's productivity, but it is self-fruitful so a single tree will crop without a second pollinator nearby.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile soil sheltered from strong wind, since white sapote wood is somewhat brittle. Chestnut is a vigorous, heavy-cropping California selection that produces round, yellow-green fruit with smooth, custard-textured flesh recalling banana and caramel once fully ripe, though the skin itself carries a persistent bitterness and should not be eaten. Its firmer flesh holds up to handling and shipping better than many softer-fleshed sapote selections, making it a good choice for growers who want fruit that survives a trip from the yard to the kitchen intact. Allow harvested fruit to soften fully at room temperature for several days before eating, and prune young trees to a strong scaffold framework, since mature trees can become large and top-heavy without early shaping.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — White Sapote Fruit Facts
University of Florida IFAS Extension — White Sapote Growing in the Home Landscape
University of California Cooperative Extension, Ventura County — White Sapote

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring; in zone 9b–10 plant March–May. Trompo is a University of Florida-selected canistel valued for unusually large fruit and heavy bearing, with young trees needing frost protection for their first two winters.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to sandy soil; Trompo takes its name from the distinctive top-shaped (trompo) form of its fruit, which is noticeably larger than typical seedling canistel, often 8-15 ounces, with smooth yellow skin and dense, deep-orange pulp. The texture is drier and more custard-like than most tree fruit, frequently compared to sweet potato or pumpkin pie filling, and is popular blended into milkshakes and flans throughout South Florida. Trees bear heavily through winter with an occasional light summer crop, so thin small fruit clusters on young trees to avoid limb breakage from the fruit's substantial weight. Harvest when the skin turns fully glossy yellow-orange and let fruit finish softening at room temperature for several days, since canistel is unpalatable until fully soft.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Canistel Growing in the Home Landscape
Florida State Horticultural Society Proceedings — Pouteria campechiana Cultivar Notes
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Canistel and Related Pouteria Species

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9b–10 plant March–May in the most frost-protected microclimate available and shield young trees with frost cloth for the first several winters. J-31 is a Malaysian-origin selection widely planted in South Florida for its exceptional eating quality.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, since jackfruit roots are very intolerant of standing water. J-31 produces large, irregularly lobed fruit with firm, deep-yellow flesh and a sweet, rich flavor and aroma that South Florida tropical fruit tasters consistently rank among the best of any named jackfruit selection, with bulbs that separate cleanly and rarely turn mushy or split on the tree. The tree has an open, spreading, fast-growing habit but responds well to pruning, allowing it to be kept to roughly 15 feet for easier harvest and home garden management. Established trees are prolific, often producing fruit outside the normal summer-to-fall season as well as during it, so support developing fruit on young limbs with slings to prevent limb breakage under the fruit's considerable weight.
sources: Florida State Horticultural Society Proceedings — New Jackfruit Cultivars for Commercial and Dooryard Planting
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Jackfruit Growing in the Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Jackfruit Cultivar Evaluations

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9b–10 plant in the warmest, most frost-sheltered microclimate and protect young trees for their first several winters. NS1 was among the first superior jackfruit selections established in the Western Hemisphere and is prized for its compact, precocious habit.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; NS1 forms a dense, upright, medium-vigor canopy that stays far more compact than seedling jackfruit and can be held to roughly 8-10 feet with routine annual pruning, making it one of the more manageable named selections for a home dooryard. Trees are heavy, reliable bearers, and fruit are dark green and blocky with blunt, flattened spines that open as the fruit ripens, enclosing firm, dark-orange flesh with a rich, sweet flavor. Because NS1 begins fruiting on relatively young, small trees, thin the first one or two crops to just a few fruit per tree so the young trunk and root system can establish before carrying a full load. Harvest when the spines flatten and the fruit develops a hollow sound when tapped, then let it finish ripening at room temperature for a day or two before cutting.
sources: Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden Virtual Herbarium — Jackfruit Cultivar Descriptions
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Jackfruit Growing in the Home Landscape
Florida State Horticultural Society Proceedings — Jackfruit Cultivar Evaluations

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Black Pearl requires warm, humid, essentially frost-free conditions (zone 10b-12) to fruit reliably and is self-pollinating, so a single tree will set a crop.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with steady moisture, since wax apple fruit quality and size drop sharply under drought stress. Black Pearl is one of the most sought-after wax apple selections grown in Taiwan, prized for fruit that ripens to a deep purplish-red, almost black skin, noticeably darker than standard pink or red wax apple types, enclosing crisp, juicy, mildly sweet flesh with the characteristic hollow, rose-scented core. Compared to seedling wax apple trees, Black Pearl grows in a shorter, more compact form that is easier to net against birds and harvest without a ladder. Pick fruit by hand as soon as the skin reaches full color, since ripe wax apple does not continue to sweeten after picking and bruises easily, and keep young trees well mulched and watered through their first two dry seasons to establish a strong root system.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops — Wax Apple (Fruits of Warm Climates)
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tropical Fruits for South Florida
Taiwan Council of Agriculture — Wax Apple Production Notes
